text: Aurangzeb ruled for nearly fifty years and pushed the empire to its largest size ever.
But he spent his last twenty-five years at war in the south, and he brought back the
jizya tax.
His toughest enemy was a young Maratha leader from the hills near Pune, Shivaji, a master
of fast raids and hill forts.
Placed under house arrest in Agra, he escaped, as the famous story goes, hidden inside giant
baskets of sweets.
After Aurangzeb died in 1707, the empire cracked.
Governors became kings.
The Marathas spread across the center of India.
And in 1739, the Persian ruler Nadeer Shah marched in and sacked Delhi.
He carried home the Peacock Throne, and the Koei Noor.
Remember Mahmoud's camels?

On the last day of 1600, Queen Elizabeth I gave a charter to a group of London merchants,
the East India Company.
At first, they just wanted to trade, and what they wanted most was that Indian cloth, painted
printed cotton so popular in England that its names entered the English language, Calico
from Calicut, and Chintz from the Hindi Chint.
It sold so well that English weavers rioted and Parliament passed laws to ban Indian printed
cloth. The company set up trading posts at Seward, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta. Bombay,
by the way, came to England as part of a royal wedding dowry when a Portuguese princess
married King Charles II. Imagine getting Mumbai as a wedding gift. To protect its trade,
